**Notes**: `visible(boolean)` is a Pathland extra (SwiftUI only has
`.hidden()` — `Visible`/`Hidden`). `accessibilityRole`/`accessibilityState`
take raw `int` codes today rather than a typed enum. Raw input listeners are
exposed through the `PointerEvents` modifier value — there is no per-event sugar
(e.g. a `.focusable` or `.onSubmit` that sets the matching bit). `environment`
is the one inheritance/scoping modifier
([§6 rule 6](#6-authoring-conventions)), alongside the style modifiers.

**Window metadata is root-scoped.** `windowMetadata` applies to the whole
hosting surface, not to the subtree it wraps. Values are signals (a plain value
is wrapped as a constant), so a route's title is a `computed` over the router:
`windowMetadata(w -> w.title(computed(() -> titleFor(router.path()))))`. A
signal change re-emits only that `META::SET_WINDOW_METADATA` field; the renderer
maps it to the window/tab title and description.

### 5.6 Custom modifiers (developer-authored)

In SwiftUI any developer can define a modifier that applies to **any** existing
view — and Pathland is the same. This is a **first-class, MUST** property of
every conformant DSL: modifiers are never hard-bound to a view type.

- **Applicable to any view.** A modifier works on a library primitive
  (`Text`), a container (`VStack`), a control (`Button`), a custom view, or an
  already-modified view. The same modifier value applies everywhere.
- **One mechanism.** Core and application-authored modifiers are the **same
  surface**: a `ViewModifier` value applied via `.modifiers(...)`. There is
  **no per-modifier sugar on the view type**; a parameterized modifier is
  constructed by a lowercase static function named for the modifier ([§5.0](#50-authoring-a-modifier))
  and single-value modifiers pass the value directly.

| | Canonical | Java DSL (`com.pathland.view`) | Rust DSL (`pathland-view`) |
|-|-----------|-------------------------------|----------------------------|
| authoring | `struct Card: ViewModifier { func body(content: Content) -> some View }` | `@FunctionalInterface ViewModifier { View body(View content) }` | `trait ViewModifier { fn apply(&mut Node) }` |
| applying | `content.modifier(Card())` | `content.modifiers(card(c -> …))` / `content.modifiers(A, B)` | `content.modifiers(Card)` |
| single-value | `.modifier(Padding(16))` | `content.modifiers(padding(p -> p.uniform(16)))` | `content.modifiers(Padding(16.0))` |

**Composition**: a custom modifier composes core modifiers **or** wraps
`content` with additional structure (a background, an overlay, a frame) and
returns the decorated view — exactly SwiftUI's `body(content: Content)`.

**Emission contract**: a custom modifier composed from core modifiers emits the
same one-`SET_PROPERTY`-per-property deltas as writing the modifiers inline;
emission stays diff-based, and a renderer that cannot apply a modifier
**allows and ignores** it.

**Realization deltas**:
- **Rust** — every core modifier (`Padding`, `FontSize`, `ForegroundStyle`,
  `Frame`, …) implements `ViewModifier`, and `.modifiers(...)` applies them
  (a single modifier or a tuple).
  Caveat: `apply(&mut Node)` mutates the built node's properties only — it
  cannot wrap `content` with new structure (the Java/SwiftUI `body(content)`
  form can). A conformant DSL's custom-modifier mechanism should support
  wrapping.
- **Java** — every core modifier is a `ViewModifier` value applied via
  `.modifiers(...)`; `View` has no modifier sugar, and a style
  (`ButtonStyle`, …) is itself a `ViewModifier` value (it binds the
  `Environment.BUTTON_STYLE` key down the subtree — subtree scoping is
  environment-only). Application-authored `ViewModifier.body(View)` is
  SwiftUI-shaped and can wrap content with structure.

#### Media (`MediaController`)

A media playback is a **state object**, not a view (spec/MEDIA.md; the SwiftUI
`AVPlayer` analog). `MediaController` owns the transport as signals — commands
(`source()`, `playing()`, `position()`, `volume()`, `muted()`, `loop()`,
`rate()`) and reports (`time()`, `duration()`, `volumeReport()`) — plus
`play()/pause()/toggle()/seek()/setVolume()`. The emitter materializes one
non-visual `MEDIA_CONTROLLER` node per controller (keyed by object identity), so
playback is stable across structural swaps.

- **Audio has no view**: bind ordinary views (buttons/sliders) to the
  controller's signals. Include `controller.attach()` once in the tree — a
  non-visual marker that materializes the controller node — placed **outside**
  any swapping branch (e.g. a `SizeThatFits` slot).
- **Video** is the only media view: `Video.make(controller)` renders the
  controller's output. `VideoStyle` supplies a custom control surface; the
  default `NativeVideoStyle` shows renderer-native controls.
- A `MediaController` may be rebound to the app's own (e.g. persisted) signals
  (`controller.playing(signal)`), so the controller drives the same state the
  rest of the UI reads.

```java
MediaController player = new MediaController(computed(() -> track.get().audio()));
player.playing(playing.signal()).position(seekRequest.signal()).volume(volume.signal());
player.time(position.signal()).onEnded(this::next);

VStack.make().children(
    player.attach(),                                   // audio: non-visual
    Button.make(b -> b.action(player::toggle)),
    Slider.make(s -> s.value(player.time())),
    Video.make(player));                               // video: the only media view
```

## 5.7 Styleable controls (the style contract)

A **style** customizes a view or control's *content*; the control owns its
*component and interaction*. This is one contract for every styleable surface
(`ButtonStyle`, `LabelStyle`, `VideoStyle`, …), and it is the
author-facing shape of the protocol's **Composite Override Mode**
([PRIMITIVES.md §2](./PRIMITIVES.md#2-dual-mode-rendering-pipeline--platform-delegation)).

- **The control owns the native component and the interaction.** A semantic
  control renders its **native control node** (its component id — `BUTTON`,
  `VIDEO`, …) and attaches its behavior to *that* node: the tap action /
  `EVENT_LISTENERS` (Button), the value/text/date sink, or the media binding
  (`Video`). The **whole control is interactive**, including its padding.
- **The style owns the content.** A style returns the control's **content view**
  from `makeBody(Config)`; the control attaches it as the control node's
  **single child**. The content keeps its own component(s), layout, and
  properties — a style **never** sets or overwrites the control's component and
  never wires the interaction. The result is a control with children → protocol
  **Composite Override Mode**.
- **The style consumes the control's config.** The `Config` a style's
  `makeBody(Config)` receives is the **same type** the view configured through
  `make(...)` ([§2](#2-canonical-signature-notation)): `ButtonStyle.makeBody(Button.Config)`,
  `LabelStyle.makeBody(Label.Config)`,
  `VideoStyle.makeBody(VideoStyle.Configuration)`. The style **reads** the config (the
  control's values: content, action, label, media state); it does not mutate it.
- **A style is a modifier.** Styles are `ViewModifier` values scoped down a
  subtree with `.modifiers(<Style>)`, binding the style's `EnvironmentKey` over
  the wrapped subtree (nearest wins); the control reads it via its
  `Environment.<name>Style()` accessor. This is the one inheritance mechanism
  ([§6 rule 6](#6-authoring-conventions)); `ButtonStyle` binds
  `Environment.BUTTON_STYLE`, `VideoStyle` `Environment.VIDEO_STYLE`, `LabelStyle`
  `Environment.LABEL_STYLE`.
- **Button content precedence (three developer options).** A `Button`'s content
  resolves as: (1) an **explicit child** supplied via `.children(...)` wins;
  else (2) the config **title** string (wrapped as a `Text`); else (3) the
  **style-supplied content** from `makeBody`. The `buttonStyle` modifier itself
  (option 3) lets a developer hand content in through the style. This mirrors
  SwiftUI's multiple button-authoring forms.
- **Defaults preserve the native path.** The default style contributes the
  control's natural content: `PlainButtonStyle` → the label;
  `NativeVideoStyle` → **no content** (an empty-content
  sentinel), so the control stays a **leaf** in Native Token Mode and the
  renderer shows native media controls; `DefaultLabelStyle` → title + icon.
- **Text/foreground modifiers cascade to content.** A `.foregroundStyle`/
  `.fontSize` (and the other inherited text modifiers) applied *to the control*
  reach the content's text — SwiftUI environment semantics. In the Java DSL the
  properties ride the control node; renderers cascade them to child text.
- **Main-axis alignment is the content's own layout — no protocol property.**
  A control's content box centers its child by default; to left-align a
  composite label (e.g. a navigation row), make the label full-width
  (`frame(f -> f.width(FILL))`) and let its own `ALIGNMENT` place its
  content. There is deliberately no main-axis/justification property (the engine
  describes WHAT, never WHERE — [§1](#1-design-principles-dsl-flavored)).
- **Closed-variant ("token") styles are the same surface, not a wrapper.** Some
  styles select a whole native variant rather than supplying content:
  `ToggleStyle`/`PickerStyle`/`TextStyle` are wire **enums** applied as
  properties (`TOGGLE_STYLE`, …), and `LabelStyle` shapes which parts render.
  They are scoped/read exactly like the wrapper styles above.

Canonical signatures (SwiftUI-shaped) and the realization:

| Control | Style protocol | `Config` | Default style |
|---------|----------------|----------|---------------|
| `Button` | `ButtonStyle { makeBody(config) -> View }` | the `Button.Config` (title, action, content) | `PlainButtonStyle` (label) |
| `Label` | `LabelStyle { makeBody(config) -> View }` | the `Label.Config` (title, icon) | `DefaultLabelStyle` (title + icon) |
| `Video` | `VideoStyle { makeBody(config) -> View }` | the `VideoStyle.Configuration` (its `MediaController`) | `NativeVideoStyle` (no content) |

```java
// Button: the control wires the action; the style decorates the label/content.
enum MyButtonStyle implements ButtonStyle { INSTANCE;
    @Override public View makeBody(Button.Config c) {
        return c.content().modifiers(padding(p -> p.uniform(12)), background(b -> b.color(BLUE)));
    }
}
Button.make(b -> b.title("Save").action(this::save)).modifiers(MyButtonStyle.INSTANCE);

// Label: the style decides which parts render (nullable parts = absent).
enum BadgeLabelStyle implements LabelStyle { INSTANCE;
    @Override public View makeBody(Label.Config c) {
        return HStack.make().children(
                c.icon().modifiers(frame(f -> f.width(18).height(18))),
                c.title());
    }
}
```

The Java DSL ships `PlainButtonStyle`/`BorderedButtonStyle`,
`DefaultLabelStyle`/`TitleOnlyLabelStyle`/`IconOnlyLabelStyle`, and
`NativeVideoStyle`; application-authored styles implement the
same interfaces. **Delta:** SwiftUI's `LabelStyleConfiguration.title`/`.icon`
are always-present views; Pathland passes `null` for an absent part (a style
checks `hasTitle()`/`hasIcon()`). Because styles are modifiers, a style is
applied with `.modifiers(<Style>)`.

---

## 6. Authoring conventions

A conformant DSL follows these conventions:

1. **Names**: SwiftUI view/modifier names; per-language case (camelCase,
   snake_case). `foregroundStyle` not `foregroundColor`; `fontWeight`,
   `multilineTextAlignment`, `scaledToFit`, `allowsHitTesting` keep their
   SwiftUI spellings. A modifier's type is **never** suffixed `Mod`.
2. **Signature order**: canonical parameter order is preserved —
   `.border(color, width)`, `.frame(width, height, alignment)`,
   `.shadow(color, radius, x, y)`. Compound modifiers expand to one property
   per argument.
3. **Values vs modifiers**: structural/layout values and a control's bound value
   are configured through a view's `make(...)` (modifiers through lowercase
   functions); everything else is a chainable `modifiers(...)` value. The three
   operations may be chained in any order.
4. **Typed enums**: `HorizontalAlignment` (leading/center/trailing, for
   `VStack`), `VerticalAlignment` (top/center/bottom, for `HStack`), `Alignment`
   (2D — topLeading … bottomTrailing — for `ZStack`/grids and the `frame`
   modifier's content alignment); all **position-only, never stretching** (a
   child's `FILL` size kind stretches). Plus `TextAlignment`, `FontWeight`
   (100–900), `Truncation` (head/middle/tail),
   `TextCase` (none/uppercase/lowercase), `FontStyle` (normal/italic),
   `FontDesign` (default/serif/rounded/monospaced), `ContentMode` (fit/fill),
   `ControlSize` (small/regular/large), `ToggleStyle`
   (switch/checkbox/button), `PickerStyle` (menu/segmented/wheel/radiogroup),
   `DatePickerMode` (date/time/dateAndTime), `ShapeKind`
   (circle/rectangle/roundedRectangle/capsule/ellipse/path). Numeric codes
   come from MODIFIERS.md's appendix; the DSL resolves them.
5. **`Spacer`/`Color` as views**: `Spacer` is a flexible expanding filler;
   `Color` in a tree is a layout-greedy fill.
6. **The environment is the only inheritance mechanism.** Any value that must
   reach a whole subtree — a style (`ButtonStyle`), the router, the active path,
   the session's persisted state — is injected through the environment, never
   threaded through constructors and never through a second scoping system. The
   environment is a hierarchical, nearest-wins scope of typed `EnvironmentKey`
   values (the `EnvironmentBinding` modifier value / `Environment.value(key)`,
   Java; §4.5). A language MAY implement the scope with a thread-local over the
   synchronous render pass (Java does) — but that is the implementation of the
   one mechanism, not an additional one. A subtree-scoping modifier MUST be
   expressed as an `EnvironmentKey` binding: `ButtonStyle` binds
   `Environment.BUTTON_STYLE` (`EnvironmentKey<ButtonStyle>`), exactly like the
   router and the active path.
7. **Reactivity discipline**: `body()` is a tracked render; a signal read there
   subscribes the component and a later write re-renders that component, whose
   subtree is diffed into deltas. A bound node stays fine-grained (one delta, no
   body re-run). Never write signals during render. Non-signal reads are
   mount-time only ([§3.4](#34-structural-reactivity-reactive-bodies--slots)).
8. **Emission contract**: each DSL call emits exactly the documented
   properties with the documented value types; the emitter diffs. The DSL never
   computes layout, never positions, never serializes full trees.

---

## 7. Theme management

Pathland theming is **application-owned over a renderer-owned token system**
([TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md); the wire encoding lives in [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md)
§Design Token System). The DSL gives the author two distinct surfaces:

1. **Token references in style modifiers** — semantic intent instead of a
   literal: `foregroundStyle(f -> f.color(Color.token("color.primary")))`
   emits a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference the renderer resolves against the current
   scheme. No opcode is re-emitted when a token or the scheme changes.
2. **Global theme overrides** — a batch of `PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` commands
   rolled at mount: a single-scheme `Theme` or an `AdaptiveTheme` light+dark
   pair (base = **light**, `dark.`-prefixed = **dark**).

> **Ownership**: the application owns theme values (base + `dark.*`) and token
> references; the renderer owns token defaults (light + dark), effective
> color-scheme detection, resolution (override → default → parent → fallback),
> and interaction-state styling (hover/pressed/focus/disabled). The protocol
> never transmits hover/click/transition styling.

### 7.1 Token-typed values

Any property whose value type is `COLOR` / `F32` / `STRING` / `ENUM` MAY carry a
**token reference** instead of a literal value (MODIFIERS.md §Value types). The
reference rides the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type (`0x08`) with the token path in
the arena — **never** a packed literal. A property carries exactly one value
(literal or reference, never both).

| Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Java DSL | Rust DSL | Emits |
|----------------------------|----------|----------|-------|
| `Color.token("color.primary")` | `Color.token("color.primary")` | `Color::token("color.primary")` | `DESIGN_TOKEN` ref (`0x08`) in any COLOR-typed property: `COLOR` 0x100A (`.foregroundStyle`), `BACKGROUND_COLOR` 0x1001, `BORDER_COLOR` 0x1004, `SHADOW_COLOR` 0x1021, `TINT` 0x1030, … |
| `Color.token("dark.color.surface")` | `Color.token("dark.color.surface")` | `Color::token("dark.color.surface")` | same — an explicit dark-variant reference (resolves the dark layer in either scheme) |
| `.padding(space.2)` / `Spacing(space.2)` | `Padding.with(Length.token("space.2"))` / `spacing(Length.token("space.2"))` | `Padding(Length::token("space.2"))` / `spacing(Length::token("space.2"))` | `DESIGN_TOKEN` ref in a F32-typed property: `PADDING` 0x1011 / `SPACING` 0x0001 / `CONTENT_MARGINS` 0x0005, … (see TOKENS.md §Generative token families) |
| `Font.body.family` token | `FontFamily.token("font.body.family")` | `FontFamily::token("font.body.family")` | `DESIGN_TOKEN` ref in a STRING-typed property (`FONT_FAMILY`) |

Token references are **static paths**: a signal-bound property carries a
literal value, not a token reference.

`Color` keeps its dual identity: as a **View** it is a layout-greedy fill; as a
token reference (`Color.token(path)`) it is a **data value** passed to
style-taking modifiers. A token-typed property resolves renderer-side and
**re-resolves automatically** when the effective scheme changes — overrides and
scheme are renderer state, so no node is ever re-emitted for a theme/scheme
change.

Rules:

1. Reference any token path — the standard catalog (TOKENS.md §Standard Token
   Catalog) or an application-defined path. A renderer that cannot apply a token
   falls back rather than erroring.
2. `space.<N>` members are **generative**: reference them freely (`space.2`,
   `space.0.5`), but override only `space.base` (see §7.2 rule 2).
3. A token reference must not be combined with a literal on the same property.

### 7.2 Global theme overrides

A **theme** is a batch of token overrides. Every override defines **exactly one
value**; combine a light and a dark `Theme` via `AdaptiveTheme` for adaptive
theming.

| Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Java DSL (`com.pathland.view`) | Rust DSL (`pathland-view` / `pathland-engine`) | Emits |
|----------------------------|--------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|-------|
| `Theme()` — one-scheme override batch | `new Theme().color(...)...` | `Theme::new()` | one `PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` per override (`A` = arena path, `B` = valueType, `C` = value) |
| `.color("color.primary", 0xFF2563EB)` | `.color("color.primary", 0xFF2563EB)` | `.color("color.primary", 0xFF2563EB)` | `COLOR`-typed override (sRGB `0xAARRGGBB`) |
| `.f32("space.base", 4.0)` | `.f32("space.base", 4.0f)` | `.f32("space.base", 4.0)` | `F32`-typed override (lengths in device pixels) |
| `.u32("…", v)` / `.u8("…", v)` | `.u32(path, int)` / `.u8(path, int)` | `.u32(path, v)` / `.u8(path, v)` | `U32` / `U8`-typed override |
| `.string("font.body.family", "Inter")` | `.string(path, String)` | `.string(path, "Inter")` | `STRING`-typed override (arena) |
| `AdaptiveTheme(light, dark)` | `new AdaptiveTheme(light, dark)` | `AdaptiveTheme::new(light, dark)` | light overrides as base tokens; dark overrides `dark.`-prefixed |

Emission contract:

- The theme is emitted **once at mount** as a frame of
  `PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` opcodes before the tree. Java: `new Emitter(sink,
  theme)` emits it at the start of the mount and `renderFull` (resync) frames;
  Rust: `Engine::apply_theme` / `Engine::apply_adaptive_theme`.
- Overrides are **renderer state**: they never re-emit nodes and never
  participate in the diff — an unchanged tree with a theme still emits **zero**
  per-node opcodes.
- `AdaptiveTheme` emits the light `Theme`'s overrides as base paths and the dark
  `Theme`'s with the `dark.` prefix (added automatically when the author wrote a
  bare path). The renderer derives the effective scheme from the platform and
  resolves each override against it.
- The renderer supplies light + dark defaults for the whole Tier 1 catalog, so
  dark mode works even when the author only overrides base tokens.

Authoring rules:

1. Override any token in the catalog or an application-defined path; never
   assume specific renderer default values.
2. Override `space.base` to control the whole spacing scale — individual
   `space.<N>` members MUST NOT be overridden.
3. Overrides are **global and renderer-wide**: apply the theme once per
   session/host at mount, not per view.

### 7.3 Runtime theming and scheme choice

A host MAY replace the theme after mount. Replacement is **reset + apply**: the
host emits `META::RESET_THEME` followed by the new theme's
`PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides in one frame. The renderer clears the
old overrides, re-resolves every token-referencing property, and re-applies the
new values; no node is re-emitted.

The host MAY also force the effective scheme with
`META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME`:

| Canonical mode | Emits | Behavior |
|----------------|-------|----------|
| `.platform` | `SET_COLOR_SCHEME` A=0 | follow the OS/browser light/dark signal (default) |
| `.light` | `SET_COLOR_SCHEME` A=1 | force the light design |
| `.dark` | `SET_COLOR_SCHEME` A=2 | force the dark design |

While forced, platform scheme changes are ignored. Returning to `.platform`
restores native detection. Both commands are renderer state — the emitter
re-resolves, never re-emitting the tree.

Java exposes this through `Emitter.replaceTheme(...)` / `resetTheme()` /
`setColorScheme(...)`; the server runtime's host-level
`PathlandSession.setTheme(...)` / `setColorScheme(...)` delegate to the same
emission path. Rust exposes `Engine::reset_theme` / `set_color_scheme` (and
`replace_theme` / `replace_adaptive_theme`).

Now I understand. Need to plan specific implementation. Let me look at all Java view types that need Kotlin functions, and decide whether to auto-generate or handwrite. There are ~80 view/modifier files. Writing a full Kotlin facade manually is large. Could generate Kotlin top-level functions from Java via reflection? No. Could make a thin Kotlin DSL that delegates to Java and covers the required surface with hand-written code. But spec required full surface. Perhaps generate the Kotlin facade sources from a script based on Java `Modifiers.java` and view types? That's risky. But we can structure the DSL as a single Kotlin file with aliases/functions for each view and modifier. However SwiftUI ergonomics requires named parameters, trailing lambdas, etc. We can handwrite the primary views and use a generic `modifier` passthrough for the rest.

Better architecture: Kotlin DSL wraps Java `View` and re-exports the Java enums and modifiers. For each view, a top-level function with named/optional params and a trailing `content: ViewScope.() -> Unit` / vararg children. The Kotlin functions produce `View`. For modifiers, expose lowercase Kotlin functions that delegate to Java `Modifiers`. Most modifier values are single-value or config-lambda; Kotlin can call Java `Modifiers.padding(16f)` directly. SwiftUI-style `.padding(16)` requires extension on `View` that calls `.modifiers(Modifiers.padding(16f))`. But chaining `View.modifiers` returns `View` (Java default), so extension functions on `View` work. Thus:

```kotlin
fun View.padding(value: Float): View = modifiers(Modifiers.padding(value))
fun View.frame(configure: Frame.Config.() -> Unit): View = modifiers(Modifiers.frame { it.configure() })
```

But `configure: Frame.Config.() -> Unit` requires SAM conversion from Kotlin lambda to Consumer<Config>; Kotlin supports SAM conversion for Java interfaces, yes. `Modifiers.frame(Consumer<Frame.Config>)` with lambda `{ it.width(100f) }` works. But `.configure()` extension? In Kotlin, a lambda with receiver `Frame.Config.() -> Unit` can't directly be passed to `Consumer<Frame.Config>`; need `{ c -> c.configure() }` or `Modifiers.frame { c -> configure(c) }`. Fine.

Also a trailing-children builder: `VStack(spacing = 8f) { Text("a"); Text("b") }`. Function:
```kotlin
fun VStack(spacing: Float? = null, alignment: HorizontalAlignment? = null, content: ViewScope.() -> Unit): View
```
But `VStack` is a Java class; can't have a function with same name? Kotlin top-level function `fun VStack(...)` conflicts with class constructor? Kotlin resolves function vs class; function named same as class is allowed (e.g. `fun Foo()`), but calling `VStack(...)` with args will choose function if constructor not accessible (private) — Java class VStack has private constructor, so Kotlin likely sees private constructor and won't allow `VStack(...)` as constructor call, choosing function. Actually Kotlin may complain "cannot access constructor" but a function with same name is callable. Common pattern used by Kotlin DSLs (e.g. `fun FlowRow(...)`). To be safe, put builder functions in a package object and maybe name them exactly as classes. Since Java classes are `final`, Kotlin top-level functions with same name are okay (function and classifier namespaces separate? Kotlin allows class and function same name). Example: kotlinx.html has `fun HTML.foo()`. But class/function same name in same package can cause "conflicting overloads"? Let's verify from knowledge: You can declare `fun Foo()` alongside `class Foo`; inside the same file maybe ambiguous? I believe it's allowed; constructors are invoked with `Foo()` and no-arg constructor would conflict at call site. With private Java ctor, no public constructor, so function wins. But risk. Alternative name wrappers in `dev.pathland.view.kotlin` package; classes imported as aliases or referenced fully qualified. That's clean: Kotlin DSL lives in a distinct package `dev.pathland.view.dsl`, so `VStack { }` resolves to Kotlin function, not Java class (not imported). But function body needs `dev.pathland.view.VStack`. That works. Top-level functions can be named `VStack`, `Text`, etc. in `dev.pathland.view.dsl`.

But if users also want direct Java types, they can import. Fine.

Signals: use Java `WritableSignal`/`Signal`. Kotlin ergonomic:
```kotlin
val count = mutableSignalOf(0)
Text(count) // Signal<String> no; for Int use "${count.value}"
```
Need `Signal<T>.value` extension property:
```kotlin
val <T> Signal<T>.value: T get() = get()
```
and `WritableSignal<T>.value` setter:
```kotlin
var <T> WritableSignal<T>.value: T
  get() = get()
  set(v) = set(v)
```
But extension property with same name for read/write; Java get/set accessible. Also `operator fun invoke()` maybe. For `State`, use Kotlin `State<T>` wrapper? Could expose the Java `State` and property delegation:
```kotlin
fun <T> persistedState(initial: T, key: String? = null) = ...
```
But binding requires processor. For Kotlin, we can leverage Java processor via kapt + `@JvmField`. But then DSL-created views with State fields need that. # Contributing to Pathland

Thanks for your interest in Pathland — an open, cross-platform, cross-language
UI protocol. This guide covers how to build, test, and contribute.

## Code of conduct

This project is governed by the [Contributor Covenant](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). By
participating you agree to abide by its terms.

## Security

Found a vulnerability? **Do not open a public issue** — report it privately per
[SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

## Project map

- `lib/rust/` — the Rust workspace: `pathland-core` (protocol), `pathland-engine`
  (emitter/signals), `pathland-view` (DSL), `pathland-core-transport`,
  `pathland-core-capi` (C ABI), `pathland-render-gtk`, `pathland-render-html`,
  `pathland-view-native`, `pathland-render-gtk-demo`.
- `lib/java/` — the Maven reactor: `pathland-view` (`com.pathland.view`),
  `pathland-view-processor`, `pathland-render-html`, `pathland-state-redis`,
  `pathland-demo-views`, the Quarkus/Spring demos, and the TypeScript DOM
  renderer (`lib/typescript`).
- `spec/` — the protocol contract: `OPCODE.md` (primary), `PRIMITIVES.md`,
  `MODIFIERS.md`, `EVENTS.md`, `CONFORMANCE.md` (golden vectors), `DSL.md`
  (authoring surface).

Implementation status per project lives in each crate/module's `status.md`.

- **Rust**: stable toolchain (`rustup`); `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target for the
  `no_std` direction guard.
- **Java**: JDK 17+ (Maven `release=17`; the whole stack runs on every LTS from 17).
- **GTK4** (Linux) for `pathland-render-gtk`.

```bash
# Rust workspace

# no_std / wasm32 direction guard (requires: rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown)
cd lib/rust && ./check-wasm.sh

# C ABI (cdylib) used by Java JNA / native hosts

# Java reactor (the core libraries; the Quarkus/Spring demos are excluded from
# CI but buildable with: cd lib/java && mvn -q install)
cd lib/java && mvn -q -B test -pl '!pathland-quarkus-demo,!pathland-spring-boot-demo'
```

CI runs exactly these commands (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`).

1. Open an issue first (or pick an open one) so the work is visible. Issues are
   labelled by epic: `hardening`, `benchmarking`, `tooling`, `a11y-seo`,
   `packaging`, and grouped into milestones `1 · Hardening & Memory Safety`
   through `5 · Packaging & Grant Readiness`.

  golden vectors in `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` **before** implementations depend on
  the change.

# Generative AI transparency

Pathland is a **human-directed** engineering project. This statement documents how
generative AI is used in its development, in line with the [NLnet Restack GenAI
policy](https://nlnet.nl/foundation/policies/generativeAI/).

## How AI is used

- **Design decisions are human.** The architectural choices — the fixed-size ring
  buffer and 16-byte opcode slot, "declarative, not positioned", renderer
  statelessness, signal-based diff emission, the single opcode format for both
  directions, the specification and conformance vectors, and the choice of the
  first DSLs (Rust + Java) — were made and steered by the maintainer. The spec
  (`spec/`) is the authority and **locks in** accepted decisions.
- **AI assists with implementation and drafting.** Most code, tests, and
  documentation were drafted with generative-AI assistance under the maintainer's
  direction and then reviewed, validated, and integrated by the maintainer.
  Tools used: **Gemini** (high-level design brainstorming, reasoning about
  technical approaches) and **DeepSeek v4.0 Flash / Pro** (code and document
  assistance).
- **Human accountability.** The maintainer understands and can explain the design
  and code decisions, and is responsible for correctness, clarity, and
  reproducibility. AI output is never merged unexamined.

## Contribution policy

- All code is contributed under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE) and must be
  original or compatible with that license (AI-assisted contributions must not
  reproduce copyrighted or incompatible material).
- If you use AI assistance in a pull request, say so in the PR description and
  ensure a human has reviewed and understood the contribution before submitting.

request (opencode session exports; a best-effort summary of the Gemini
discussions). See also [`docs/GRANT.md`](docs/GRANT.md) §13 and
[`docs/NLNET-APPLICATION.md`](docs/NLNET-APPLICATION.md).

Now, let's think about concrete plan and questions.

Architecture choice is key. Let me weigh:

Option A: Kotlin facade over Java library (recommended)
- New Maven module `lib/java/pathland-view-kotlin` (or `lib/kotlin/pathland-view-kotlin`).
- Depends on `pathland-view` (Java DSL, signals, emitter, wire codec).
- Provides idiomatic Kotlin top-level DSL in package `dev.pathland.view.kotlin`:
  - View constructors with named args + trailing content lambdas.
  - Modifier extension functions on `View` delegating to `Modifiers`.
  - Signal ergonomics extension properties/operator.
  - ForEach with native lambda `(item, index)`; maybe inline.
  - Custom view support: `abstract class KView : View` / interface `CompositeView` using existing tracking.
  - State: property delegates + a `bindState` mechanism (need design).
  - Navigation facade wrappers.
- Tests parity: mount and compare byte output with Java golden cases.
- Biggest pro: reuses all protocol, emitter, signals, wire codec, renderers. Fast. Cons: Kotlin is composition sugar; Java final primitives and private constructors are fine via `make`. Parameter config builders are Java `Consumer`, not Kotlin named. The facade hides it.
- Kotlin users can still access Java types.

Option B: Full Kotlin reimplementation (emitter, wire codec, signals)
- Massive, duplicates Java, violates "one reference implementation per language"? No, but too big. Not recommended.

Option C: Kotlin Multiplatform (common) implementation for future native/JS
- Much larger, needs KMP Gradle build; no Gradle currently. Defer.

I will recommend A.

Then within A, State handling:
Option A1: kapt + Java annotation processor with `@JvmField` State fields — parity, auto-key by property name. Requires kotlin-maven-plugin + kapt. Test on JDK 17/21/25. kapt works on JDK 25? Kapt is being deprecated but still works. Could be fragile.
Option A2: Kotlin-native `State` delegation with explicit keys and a small `StateBinder` interface. Example:
```kotlin
class CounterView : KotlinView() {
    val count = mutableState(0) // explicit state object
    override fun body() = ...
}
```
where `mutableState` lazily binds to `env.state()` on first render via a base class hook. Actually we can design a base class `KotlinView` implementing Java `View`:
```kotlin
abstract class KotlinView : View {
    private val stateFields = mutableListOf<State<*>>()
    protected fun <T> state(initial: T, key: String? = null): State<T> { ... }
    override fun renderNode(env: Environment): PathlandNode {
        env.state()?.let { st -> stateFields.forEach { it.bind(st, ...) } }
        return View.super.renderNode? // can't call interface default easily in Kotlin
    }
}
```
Kotlin can call `View.super.renderNode(env)`? In Kotlin, to call a default method of a Java interface from a class implementing it: `super<View>.renderNode(env)` should work if `View` is a supertype. Actually Kotlin supports `super<View>` only for interface default methods implemented? Java default methods are visible; I think `super<View>.renderNode(env)` works. ## Plan: Kotlin DSL (DX-first facade)

### Architecture

Build **`lib/java/pathland-view-kotlin`** as a Kotlin facade over `pathland-view`. It reuses the Java emitter, signals, wire codec, navigation, and renderers, so Kotlin-authored trees are **byte-identical** to equivalent Java trees.

Package: `dev.pathland.view.dsl` (keeps Kotlin builders separate from the Java classes, avoiding `Text`/`VStack` class-vs-function clashes when users import only the DSL).

### DX target

```kotlin
import dev.pathland.view.View
import dev.pathland.view.dsl.*

class CounterView : KotlinView() {
    private var count by state(0)          // auto-keyed "count", no processor

    override fun body(): View = VStack(spacing = 8f) {
        Text("Count: $count")
        HStack(spacing = 4f) {
            Button("−") { count-- }
            Button("+") { count++ }
        }
    }.padding(16f)
}
```

Key ergonomics:
- `Text("…")`, `VStack { … }`, `Button("Save") { save() }` — SwiftUI-shaped names.
- Trailing blocks auto-collect children: no `.children(...)` boilerplate.
- `.padding(16f)`, `.frame(width = …)`, `.foregroundStyle(…)`, `.onTapGesture { … }` — modifier sugar, not `.modifiers(padding(…))`.
- `signal(0)`, `computed { … }`, `effect { … }`, `sig.value`, `Signal<T>.map { … }`.
- `if` / `when` / `for` inside `body()`.
- `ForEach(items) { item, index -> … }` with row auto-collection.
- `val router = navigator("/") { route(...) }`, `NavigationStack(router)`, `NavigationLink("Users", to = "/users")`.
- `Video(player)`, `player.attach()`.

### Key implementation choices

1. **Auto-registration via a scoped collector**
   - Top-level view functions register themselves into the current `VStack`/`HStack` block using a thread-local stack of child lists (same synchronous, single-threaded contract as the emitter).
   - `KotlinView`’s constructor also registers itself, so `VStack { CounterView() }` works without `.children(...)`.
   - Nested containers push/pop their own scope; a single-child `ForEach` row renders as that child, preserving Java byte output.

2. **Modifier sugar**
   - Extension functions on `View` delegate to the Java `Modifiers` facade.
   - Because `ViewBuilder.modifiers` mutates in place, `Text("a").padding(8)` works even though the builder was already auto-registered.
   - `.modifiers(...)` remains available as the escape hatch.
   - Provide common typed forms plus config-lambda forms for full reactive coverage.

3. **State**
   - `KotlinView` base class + `state(initial, key = null)` property delegate.
   - `provideDelegate` captures the property name for auto-keying.
   - At render, `KotlinView` binds delegates to `env.state()` (`PersistentState`), then runs `body()` in the tracked slot.
   - No kapt and no annotation processor.

4. **Signals**
   - Thin wrappers over `Signals` plus Kotlin conveniences: `.value`, `update`, `map`, `computed`, `effect`, `untracked`, `constant`.
   - Raw config values remain constants; signal values become bindings exactly as in Java.

Add to `lib/java/pom.xml` modules:

```

 ## Architecture: Rust Opcode Engine
 
 > The canonical core is a **Rust engine** that emits the application's
 > **declarative view structure** — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing, padding,
 > alignment — as a fixed **16-byte opcode ring buffer** into shared linear
 > memory, consumed by host renderers. View components and modifiers are written

 > **`com.pathland.view` DSL** (reusable library, Java 17+); both drive the engine
 > through the flat **native C ABI** (`pathland-view-native`) over a zero-copy shared

 ### The 16-byte Opcode Engine
 
 - Every opcode is exactly **16 bytes**: `Category (1B) | Command ID (1B) | Flags (2B) | A (4B) | B (4B) | C (4B)`, `#[repr(C, packed)]`, little-endian.
 - A 64-byte cache line holds exactly **4 opcodes** → L1-cache-friendly.
 - Opcodes live in a **ring buffer** in linear memory; the guest writes at `writeCursor`, the host reads from `readCursor`; frame boundaries via a monotonic `frameCount` in the header block.
 - **Both directions are binary**: a second **event ring** (host → guest) carries `EVENT`-category opcodes. The renderer writes raw inputs at `eventWriteCursor`; the guest drains them at `eventReadCursor`. Events are 16-byte opcodes through the engine, never a side-channel callback.
 - **Variable-length data** (strings, token paths) lives in a bump **arena**; opcodes reference entries by offset (`[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`), so every opcode stays 16 bytes. A second host-owned **event arena** mirrors this in the host → guest direction (shared-memory event strings, e.g. `TEXT_CHANGED`); over the network, host → guest strings ride the batch's string section.
 - **Window metadata** (`META::SET_WINDOW_METADATA`, field family `TITLE`/`DESCRIPTION`/`LOCALE`) carries the hosting surface's presentation metadata; renderers map it to their own chrome (browser `<title>`/meta description/`<html lang>`, GTK/Qt window title). It is root-scoped and signal-backed, so a route title is a computed over the router. Web-only artifacts (canonical/robots/sitemap) stay host-owned.
 - Spec: **`spec/OPCODE.md`** (primary) + **`spec/CONFORMANCE.md`** (golden vectors). Companion catalogs: **`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`** (views), **`spec/MODIFIERS.md`** (modifiers/properties), **`spec/EVENTS.md`** (events), **`spec/LAYOUT.md`** (frame & layout allocation contract) — draft IDs are allocated there spec-first.
 
 ### Declarative, not positioned (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The engine describes WHAT the UI is — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing,
 > padding, alignment — never WHERE it is. It does not compute layout and does
 > not emit rects.**
 
 - The engine emits **declarative structure** (`TREE` create/delete/insert/remove/move) + **constraint properties** (`PARAMETER` spacing/padding/alignment/FILL/HUG hints).
 - **Native elements everywhere**: each platform's renderer maps the opcode stream onto that platform's native elements — GTK4 widgets on desktop, DOM elements in the browser, HTML server-side — and those native elements lay themselves out.  - **Reactive emission**: emission is diff-based. Only the nodes that changed emit opcodes (property diffs via `SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_TEXT`, structural diffs via `TREE` opcodes). An unchanged tree emits **zero** opcodes. Signals in the application mark the tree dirty; the engine reconciles.

 flat world (the flat `builder`/`engine` surface) as `pathland_native_*` C
 functions with a **shared-memory ring** the host driver reads in place. Any
 language that links the dylib (Swift/Java/C# via FFI) calls the flat surface —
 no per-component wrappers — and consumes opcodes zero-copy.
 
 `pathland-core-capi` (`libpathland_core`) is the **minimal ring C ABI** for the
 Java DSL: `pathland_core_create`/`destroy`, `pathland_ring_buffer_push` (one
 raw 16-byte opcode), `pathland_core_arena_alloc`, frame boundaries, zero-copy
 `ring_ptr`/`ring_len`, and event drain/send. The Java DSL
 (`com.pathland.view.ffm`) binds it with **JNA** (lazily loaded, zero JNI) and
 owns the retained tree + diff emission itself.
 
 ### GTK4 Renderer (`pathland-render-gtk`)
 
 The desktop renderer: a single crate that owns **all** GTK/glib/pango usage and
 maps opcode frames **incrementally** onto native GTK widgets (a retained
 `id → gtk::Widget` map). Both the Rust demo and the Java demo render through
 it — the demos **never call GTK or Swing directly**:
 
 - Rust demo links `pathland-render-gtk` as an `rlib` and calls `GtkRenderer::run(...)`
   with a wake closure.
 - Java demo (`pathland-gtk-demo`) loads `pathland-render-gtk` as a `cdylib` via JNA and
   calls `pathland_gtk_run_ring(ring, on_event, width, height)` over the Java DSL's own
   `libpathland_core` ring; native inputs round-trip as `EVENT` opcodes through the shared
   ring. The renderer **writes** the events and **wakes** the host (no payload); the host
   drains the event ring itself via `pathland_core_drain_events`. Events are never
   delivered through a side-channel callback — they flow through the opcode engine.
   The demo mounts `MusicPlayerView` (the same shared views the web demos use) with the
   app-driven media contract: the renderer plays the tracks through a direct GStreamer
   `playbin` and reports `MEDIA_*` events back; the demo's web-style
   `/_pathland/assets/...` paths resolve against an extracted local asset root
   (`pathland_gtk_set_asset_root`).
 
 The renderer maps native inputs onto the raw `Event` surface via GTK4
 controllers (`Button::clicked` → pointer up, `EventControllerMotion` →
 pointer move/enter/leave), emitting events through the same `Pump::send_input`
 path.
 
 `pathland_gtk::run` passes an explicit empty argv to GTK (the process command
 line belongs to the embedding host — e.g. the JVM's `-cp`/`-D` flags — and must
 not be parsed as GTK options).
 
 ### Native Java DSL (`com.pathland.view`, in `lib/java/pathland-view`)
 
 The **hand-written, zero-dependency Java 17+ DSL** (no codegen). It is the
 SwiftUI-like authoring surface shared by desktop, Spring Boot, and Quarkus
 apps. Components and modifiers:
 
 - `View` is an **open interface** — the library ships `Text`/`Image`/`Color`/
   `Rectangle`, `VStack`/`HStack`/`ZStack`, `Spacer`, `Button`,
   `TextField(placeholder, WritableSignal<String>)`, `Video` (a
   `MediaController`'s surface), and application code (Quarkus/Spring/desktop)
   defines its own views by implementing `View`. **Media is a state object, not a
   view** (spec/MEDIA.md): `MediaController` owns the resource + transport as
   signals, a `Video` surface renders it, and **audio has no view** — the app
   binds its own buttons/sliders (`controller.attach()` materializes the
   controller's node once, outside any swapping branch, so a band swap never
   restarts playback).
 - **Custom views and styles use the configurator** (spec DSL.md §2): an
   app-authored `View` with values implements `Configurable<View.Config>`, holds a
   **`private` constructor**, and exposes
   `static ViewBuilder<View, Config> make(Consumer<Config>)`; a style
   (`ButtonStyle`/`LabelStyle`/`VideoStyle`) expose a
   **lowercase static factory** on their own type returning the style value
   (`BorderedButtonStyle.borderedButtonStyle(s -> s…)`), mirroring the library's
   `Modifiers.*` lowercase functions (e.g.
   `borderedButtonStyle(b -> b.padding(..).background(..)…)`). Creation goes
   through the configurator, never a parameterized constructor. The
   `pathland-view-processor` `ViewAuthoringProcessor` **errors** on
   public/protected constructors **with parameters** in custom `View` **and**
   `Style` implementations (no-arg roots and abstract types are exempt), so the
   convention is compile-enforced where the processor is wired
   (`annotationProcessorPaths`). The library's own views/styles follow the same
   shape (`Video`, `Text`, `BorderedButtonStyle`, …).
 - **SwiftUI-style `body()` / reactive components**: composite views declare
   `View body()` (their subtree); the library's primitives override
   `renderNode(Environment)` to materialize a `PathlandNode` (`render(Environment)` is
   the emitter entry point and must not be overridden). `body()` is a **tracked
   render function**: a signal read there subscribes that component, and a later
   write re-renders only that component and diffs its retained subtree — so plain
   `if`/`switch`/`for` over signals works. A signal **bound** to a node
   (`Text.make(t -> t.text(Signal))`) stays fine-grained and does not re-run the
   body. Non-signal reads are mount-time only; render bodies must be pure/idempotent
   and must not write signals. Each child view is a component slot; the root chain
   (body delegation, modifiers, environment/tap/navigation wrappers) is one slot.
   `View.of(Supplier<View>)` is the inline form (Java has no `if` expression);
   `ForEach.of(list | Signal<List<T>>, (item, index) -> View)` is the reactive
   list component (static lists may use streams/`for` directly).
   `NavigationContainer` / `SizeThatFits` are ordinary components. The root
   component type must stay stable across re-renders. (Rust parity is Phase 2.)
 - **Cross-language vocabulary** (spec DSL.md §9.3.1): the same anchors across
   Swift, Java, Kotlin, Rust, and TypeScript — `View`, `body`/`build`, `Signal`,
   `computed`, `State`, `ForEach`, `View.of`, `children`, `modifiers`. Use native
   control flow (`if`/`switch` in Swift/Java, `if`/`when` in Kotlin, `if`/`match`
   in Rust, ternary/`switch` in TypeScript); Java uses `View.of` only where an
   inline expression is needed. Swift is the canonical SwiftUI-shaped reference;
-  Kotlin/Swift are not implemented yet and Rust parity is Phase 2.
+  Kotlin is implemented by `lib/java/pathland-view-kotlin` (a facade over the Java
+  library), Swift is not implemented yet, and Rust parity is Phase 2.
 - **The three operations (spec DSL.md §2)**: every concrete view exposes
   `make(...)` (values — the only static; `make(Consumer<Config>)`, `make(value)`,
   `make()`), and the instance operations `.modifiers(ViewModifier...)` and
   `.children(View...)` chain on the returned builder. Java's static-vs-instance
   rule means the statics sit on the view class, the chain on the builder; a bare
   `View` value applies modifiers through the interface default
   `View.modifiers(...)`. Values are a
   fluent per-view `Config` (`VStack.make(v -> v.alignment(...).spacing(8))`,
   `Text.make(t -> t.text("hi"))`); modifiers are `ViewModifier` values built by
   the **`Modifiers` facade's lowercase functions** — one
   `import static com.pathland.view.Modifiers.*;` brings the whole modifier
   vocabulary (`padding(p -> p.uniform(16))`, `frame(f -> f.width(100))`,
   `borderedButtonStyle(b -> …)`) — or, for single values, the value itself
   (`FontWeight.BOLD`, `Font.headline()`, a `ButtonStyle`). The `View` interface has
   **no per-modifier sugar** (`font`/`navigate`/`environment`/`onPathChange` were
   removed — use `.modifiers(Font…)`, `.modifiers(NavigationIntent.navigate(…))`,
   `.modifiers(environmentBinding(e -> e.key(…).value(…)))`,
   `.modifiers(pathChange(p -> p.listener(…)))`), and the `*Mod` shims
   (`EnvironmentMod`→`EnvironmentBinding`, `router/NavigationMod`→`NavigationIntent`,
   `PathChangeMod`→`PathChange`, `FontWeightMod`→`FontWeight`, …) are **removed**.
 - **Single-value shortcuts (spec DSL.md §2)**: a view/modifier whose config has a
   designated primary member also exposes a single-value construction overload that
   is pure sugar for the lambda — views construct with `make(value)` / `make(Signal<T>)`
   (`Text.make("hi")`), modifiers with the lowercase function's value form
   (`padding(16)`, `fontSize(sizeSignal)`). Multi-member configs (`Padding.edges`, `Offset`,
   `Gauge`, `Border`, …) have **no** shortcut — use the lambda. The shortcut delegates
   to the same `make(Consumer<Config>)` (views) / `Modifiers` facade
   (modifiers) factory via the package-private
   `Configurators` helper (one construction path). The former `.of(...)` construction
   factories are **removed** — a shortcut (or the lambda / `.children(...)` / empty
   `make()` for config-less views) replaces every one. Only data/branch factories keep
   `of`: `Color.of/rgb/argb/token`, `Fit.of`, `View.of`, `ForEach.of`,
   `EnvironmentKey.of`, `Route.of`, `Params.of`, `Signals.*`.
   Sizing is the `Frame` modifier value
   (`frame(f -> f.width(w).height(h).alignment(..))` and the lambda
   configurator `frame(f -> f.minWidth(..).maxWidth(..).alignment(..))`
   (min/ideal/max bounds)); all
   compile to the same `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT`/`ALIGNMENT`/min-max `SET_PROPERTY`s.
   Typed enums
   (`Alignment`/`TextAlignment`/`FontWeight`/`Truncation`), not raw ints.
 - **Environment scoping via a `ThreadLocal`** (Java 17+): a `ButtonStyle` modifier
   injects a style down the whole child tree; `ButtonStyle.makeBody(Configuration)`
   with built-in `PlainButtonStyle` / `BorderedButtonStyle`. Custom wrappers via
   `ViewModifier.body(View)`. The `Environment` also carries the session's
   `PersistentState`.
 - **Reactivity (Angular parity)** in `com.pathland.view.signal`:
   `Signals.signal/computed/effect/untracked` — lazy+memoized computeds,
   glitch-free synchronous flush, equality suppression, error caching, write
   discipline (`allowWrites()`), circular-dependency detection.
 - **Persisted view state** (`com.pathland.view.state`): a `State<T>` field (e.g.
   `State<Integer> count = new State<>(0);`) is auto-wired to the session's
   `PersistentState` (keyed by field name, or `new State<>(0, "key")` for an explicit
   key) by the `pathland-view-processor` annotation processor, which detects `State`
   fields by type and generates a `<View>_StateBinder` per view class. Each view
   connects its own `State` when it renders (`View.render` calls `Environment.state()
   → PersistentState.connect(view)`), so nested views can be instantiated inline in
   `body()` and need not be declared as fields. `PersistentState.signal(name, initial)`
   auto-loads the persisted value and auto-saves on change (key `name:scope`), and
   `StateStore` is untyped (one store serves all signal types).
 - **Fine-grained emitter** (`com.pathland.view.emit`): mounts a view tree once,
   assigns stable ids, and registers a **node-level binding effect** per reactive
   text/property — a signal change re-emits only that node's `SET_TEXT` /
   `SET_PROPERTY` (unchanged signals emit zero opcodes). Sinks: `FrameOpcodeSink`
   (self-contained frames for SSR/WebSocket) and `RingOpcodeSink` (JNA into
   `libpathland_core`). The wire codec (`com.pathland.view.transport`) mirrors
   `pathland_core_transport` (`PLPL` batch format, self-contained frames + events).
 
 Consistency with `pathland_core::constants` is enforced by the emitter/HTML
 tests (golden byte layout + round-trips), replacing the old codegen assert pass.
 
 - **Single signal value convention**: a view or modifier holds **one `Signal<T>`
   field** for a reactive value — never a raw field *plus* a signal field for the
   same value. Static values are authored through the raw config setter (or the
   `.of(T)` convenience), which
   wraps them in `Signals.constant(...)` (e.g. `Text.make(t -> t.text("Hello"))` ≡
   `Text.make(t -> t.text(Signals.constant("Hello")))`); the emitter treats a
   `ConstantSignal` as
   a plain, non-reactive property (no binding/effect), so statics carry zero
   binding overhead. Controls' config fields for *distinct* properties
   (`min`/`max`/`step`/`placeholder`/`mode`/`style`) stay raw.

 ## Project Vision
 
 **Pathland is a cross-platform, cross-language UI protocol** that enables retained-mode UI development with multiple renderer backends. It is **protocol-first**, meaning the protocol specification is the source of truth, not any particular implementation.
 
 **Primary Goal**: Write once, run anywhere - Enable UI code to be written once and deployed across web, mobile, desktop, and embedded platforms through different renderer implementations.
 
 **Status**: The Rust opcode engine (16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, diff-based reactive emission) is implemented and tested (`cargo test`). See the Architecture section above.
 
 ---
 
 ## CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
 
 ### Principle 1: Renderer Statelessness (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The renderer MUST NOT retain application state.**
 
 - Renderers are **pure functions** of the opcode stream: same opcodes → same output
 - A renderer MAY retain its **rendered-output tree** (id → native element + computed layout) for drawing, hit-testing, and event routing — this is a cache of its own output, not state
 - The renderer MUST NOT retain component property values as business state, application control flow, or anything the application can change without emitting an opcode
 - The application owns the canonical retained UI tree
 - The engine emits **deltas only**; the renderer applies them to its native elements
 
 **Violation of this principle is a bug, not a feature.**
 
 ### Principle 2: Command-Based Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol transmits tree mutations as a stream of commands, NOT as serialized trees.**
 
 - Each frame is a **batch of delta commands** describing changes
 - Only **actual changes** are transmitted (diff-based reactive emission)
 - Protocol acts like a **VM instruction stream** / ABI
 - Deterministic, linear decoding without schema lookup or reflection
 
 ### Principle 3: Binary Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol MUST be binary.**
 
 - Open-source, cross-platform binary format
 - Fixed **16-byte instructions** in a ring buffer shared with the host via linear memory
 - Custom instruction-based bytecode, not schema-driven serialization
 - **Both directions are binary**: tree mutations (app → renderer) AND raw-input events (renderer → app) share the same instruction format, so the wire is language- and platform-agnostic

 ### Opcode Format
 
 Every opcode is exactly 16 bytes:
 
 ```
 [Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
 ```
 
 See `spec/OPCODE.md` for the full format, ring buffer, arena, and frame lifecycle.
 
 ### Categories
 
 | Category | Value | Direction | Description |
 |----------|-------|-----------|-------------|
 | TREE | 0x01 | Guest → Host | Node create/delete/insert/remove/move |
 | PARAMETER | 0x02 | Guest → Host | Constraint properties (spacing, padding, …), design tokens |
 | EVENT | 0x03 | Host → Guest | Raw inputs: pointer down/move/up, key down/up |
 | META | 0x04 | Both | Reset, environment, window metadata |
 
 ### Component Types (u16)
 
 Grouped ranges (see `spec/PRIMITIVES.md`):
 
 | Group | Component | ID |
 |-------|-----------|----|
 | **Primitive Drawing (0x01–0x0F)** | TEXT | 0x01 |
 | | IMAGE | 0x02 |

 | | DIVIDER | 0x05 |
 | | SPACER | 0x06 |

 | **Layout & Container (0x10–0x1F)** | VSTACK | 0x10 |
 | | HSTACK | 0x11 |

 ### Key Property IDs
 
 **Stack**: SPACING=0x0001, ALIGNMENT=0x0002, CONTENT_MARGINS=0x0005  
 **Text**: TEXT=0x000A, TEXT_ALIGNMENT=0x000C, LINE_LIMIT=0x000B, TRUNCATION_MODE=0x000D  
 **Style**: COLOR=0x100A, FONT_SIZE=0x1007, FONT_WEIGHT=0x1008, FONT_FAMILY=0x1009, BACKGROUND_COLOR=0x1001, BORDER_WIDTH=0x1003, BORDER_COLOR=0x1004, BORDER_RADIUS=0x1005, OPACITY=0x100D, VISIBLE=0x100E, Z_INDEX=0x100F, CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS=0x1010, PADDING=0x1011, PADDING_TOP/RIGHT/BOTTOM/LEFT=0x1012-0x1015  
 **Special**: WIDTH=0x100B (use -1=FILL, -2=HUG_CONTENT), HEIGHT=0x100C  
 **Semantic**: ROLE=0x2001, STATE=0x2002, ENABLED=0x2003, SELECTED=0x2004, EVENT_LISTENERS=0x2005 (u32 bitmask — which raw events a node wants reported), VALUE=0x2006, MIN_VALUE=0x2007, MAX_VALUE=0x2008, LABEL=0x200A, PROMPT=0x200B  
 **Binding/action**: ACTION_ID=0x2016, BINDING_ID=0x2017, TOGGLE_STYLE=0x2018 (Switch=0, Checkbox=1, Button=2)  
 **Media** (spec/MEDIA.md): MEDIA_CONTROLLER_ID=0x103A (a `VIDEO`'s controller), MEDIA_SOURCE=0x103B, MEDIA_MUTED=0x103C, MEDIA_LOOP=0x103D, MEDIA_RATE=0x103E; PLAYBACK_STATE=0x1035 / MEDIA_POSITION=0x1036 / MEDIA_VOLUME=0x1037 live on the controller
 
 ### Colors
 
 - Literal colors are **sRGB** with D65 white point, packed as `0xAARRGGBB`
 - A color property may instead carry a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference to a token path
 - Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation are **renderer-owned**
 
 ### Design Token System
 
 **Core Principle**: Application defines intent, overrides, and the theme.
 Renderer defines visual appearance, behavior, defaults, and interaction states.
 
 - The **application owns the theme**: token overrides (base = **light**, `dark.`-prefixed = **dark**) and token references in style properties. Token refs cover COLOR and non-color values (`Length` for spacing/padding/font size/radius/border/frame; `FontFamily.Token` for STRING) in the Rust and Java DSLs.
 - The **renderer owns** default token values (light + dark, the full Tier-1 catalog), token resolution (including explicit `dark.` = forced dark and parent fallback), effective color-scheme detection, interaction states (hover, pressed, focus, disabled), and theme adaptation
 - `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` identifies tokens by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`) with the standard value-type encoding — there is no separate numeric tokenId system. A `dark.` prefix selects the dark variant (`dark.color.primary`); a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference whose path starts with `dark.` forces the dark value in either scheme
 - **Runtime theming**: `META::RESET_THEME` clears every app override; a replacement theme is reset + `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides in one frame. `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME` forces `platform`/`light`/`dark`. Both are renderer state — no node is re-emitted. Java: `Emitter.replaceTheme`/`setColorScheme` + `PathlandSession.setTheme`/`setColorScheme`; Rust: `Engine::reset_theme`/`set_color_scheme`.
 - An unresolvable token reference leaves the property **unset** (renderer default), never an error or stale value.
 - The protocol MUST NEVER describe hover styles, click styles, visual transitions, conditional styling, or layout tuning for interaction states
 - **Deferred**: applying per-component tokens to native GTK/Qt leaf control chrome; web parent-path fallback.
 
 The HTML renderer's default token values are generated from `design/` (see
 "HTML base design" above). Full details: [Design Token System](./spec/OPCODE.md#design-token-system)
 and the canonical catalog / color-scheme contract in [spec/TOKENS.md](./spec/TOKENS.md).

 ## Implementation Guidelines
 
 ### Adding New Component
 1. Add to `component_type` in `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Implement the component type in `pathland-core` (if it affects the retained tree)
 4. Implement native-element mapping in the target renderer (Goal 3–5)
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Adding New Property
 1. Add to the appropriate property module in `constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Handle the value type in `pathland-core`'s diff emission (if a stack/text/size property)
 4. Implement in each renderer's property application
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Modifying Protocol
 1. Update `spec/OPCODE.md` first (and `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` vectors)
 2. Update `constants.rs` and `pathland-core` encoding/emitters
 3. Verify backward compatibility; update `pathland-core`/`pathland-render-gtk` + tests
 4. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Changing the Wire Format
 - Bump the wire `version` field in `spec/OPCODE.md` and `pathland-core`'s header (currently 1). Pre-release format changes are acceptable while version stays 1.
 
 ### Keeping implementation status updated (MANDATORY)
 
 **The agent MUST keep the per-project `status.md` files in sync with the code.**
 Whenever you land a protocol or renderer change — a new component/property/
 command/event, a new encoder/decoder, a new widget mapping, a new modifier or
 renderer feature, a test that proves new surface — **update the affected
 project's `status.md`** (Implemented / Not implemented / gaps) in the same
 change. The specs (`spec/`) describe the protocol contract only and MUST NOT
 carry implementation status; status lives in `status.md` next to each
 implementing project.

 ## Common Pitfalls
 
 ### NEVER Do These
 | Anti-Pattern | Why Wrong | Correct |
 |--------------|-----------|---------|
 | Renderer stores application state | Violates statelessness | Application owns the tree |
 | Engine computes layout / emits rects | Violates declarative model | Emit structure + constraints; native elements lay out |
 | Send full trees | Inefficient | Diff-based reactive emission |
 | String property names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | String component names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | Generic RGB | Ambiguous | Explicitly sRGB |
 | Hover styles in protocol | Renderer job | Define in theme |
 | Heap allocation in steady-state emission | Slow | Preallocated snapshot slab + arena |

 ## Pathland Mindset
 
 **Always remember**:
 1. Protocol is King
 2. Renderers are Dumb (execute commands only)
 3. Applications are Smart (generate commands)
 4. Only Changes Matter (transmit mutations / reactive emission)
 5. Binary is Beautiful (efficient, deterministic)

 # Contributing to Pathland
 
 Thanks for your interest in Pathland — an open, cross-platform, cross-language
 UI protocol. This guide covers how to build, test, and contribute.
 
 ## Code of conduct
 
 This project is governed by the [Contributor Covenant](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). By
 participating you agree to abide by its terms.
 
 ## Security
 
 Found a vulnerability? **Do not open a public issue** — report it privately per
 [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
 
 ## Project map
 
 - `lib/rust/` — the Rust workspace: `pathland-core` (protocol), `pathland-engine`
   (emitter/signals), `pathland-view` (DSL), `pathland-core-transport`,
   `pathland-core-capi` (C ABI), `pathland-render-gtk`, `pathland-render-html`,
   `pathland-view-native`, `pathland-render-gtk-demo`.
 - `lib/java/` — the Maven reactor: `pathland-view` (`com.pathland.view`),
-  `pathland-view-processor`, `pathland-render-html`, `pathland-state-redis`,
-  `pathland-demo-views`, the Quarkus/Spring demos, and the TypeScript DOM
-  renderer (`lib/typescript`).
+  `pathland-view-processor`, `pathland-view-kotlin` (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`),
+  `pathland-render-html`, `pathland-state-redis`, `pathland-demo-views`, the
+  Quarkus/Spring demos, and the TypeScript DOM renderer (`lib/typescript`).
 - `spec/` — the protocol contract: `OPCODE.md` (primary), `PRIMITIVES.md`,
   `MODIFIERS.md`, `EVENTS.md`, `CONFORMANCE.md` (golden vectors), `DSL.md`
   (authoring surface).
 
 Implementation status per project lives in each crate/module's `status.md`.
 
 ## Prerequisites
 
 - **Rust**: stable toolchain (`rustup`); `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target for the
   `no_std` direction guard.
 - **Java**: JDK 17+ (Maven `release=17`; the whole stack runs on every LTS from 17).
 - **GTK4** (Linux) for `pathland-render-gtk`.
 
 ## Build & test
 
 ```bash
 # Rust workspace
 cd lib/rust && cargo test
 
 # no_std / wasm32 direction guard (requires: rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown)
 cd lib/rust && ./check-wasm.sh
 
 # C ABI (cdylib) used by Java JNA / native hosts
 cd lib/rust && cargo build -p pathland-core-capi
 
 # Java reactor (the core libraries; the Quarkus/Spring demos are excluded from
 # CI but buildable with: cd lib/java && mvn -q install)
 cd lib/java && mvn -q -B test -pl '!pathland-quarkus-demo,!pathland-spring-boot-demo'
 ```
 
 CI runs exactly these commands (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`).
 
 ## Making changes
 
 1. Open an issue first (or pick an open one) so the work is visible. Issues are
    labelled by epic: `hardening`, `benchmarking`, `tooling`, `a11y-seo`,
    `packaging`, and grouped into milestones `1 · Hardening & Memory Safety`
    through `5 · Packaging & Grant Readiness`.
 2. Create a focused branch (`fix/…`, `feat/…`, `docs/…`).
 3. Keep changes small and reviewable; add/update tests with every change.
 4. Update the relevant `status.md` file when you land protocol or renderer work
    (the specs describe the contract; implementation status lives in `status.md`).
 5. Keep commits atomic with clear messages (see below). No DCO sign-off is
    required.
 
 ## Commit style
 
 - Short, imperative subject line (`feat(view): …`, `fix(transport): …`,
   `docs(spec): …`, `refactor(…): …`).
 - Follow the repo's existing history as the style guide.
 - Reference the issue where useful (`Fixes #NN`).
 
 ## Protocol changes (important)
 
 - Update `spec/OPCODE.md` **first**, plus the affected companion catalog and the
   golden vectors in `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` **before** implementations depend on
   the change.
 - Keep the 16-byte opcode format stable; wire-format changes must bump the
   `version` field (currently 1) per `spec/OPCODE.md`.
 - New components/properties: allocate IDs in the specs + `constants.rs`
   (`lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/constants.rs`), then mirror across
   `lib/java/…/Components.java`/`Properties.java` and `lib/typescript/src/constants.ts`,
   and update each renderer + its `status.md`.
 
 ## Non-negotiable principles
 
 - Renderers are **stateless pure functions** of the opcode stream.
 - The engine emits **structure + constraints**, never positions/rects.
 - Emission is **diff-based**: only changed nodes emit; unchanged trees emit zero
   opcodes.
 - Binary both ways: tree mutations (app → renderer) and raw-input events
   (renderer → app) share the 16-byte opcode format.
 
 ## Communication
 
 - Issues/PRs are the primary channel.
 - Contact the maintainers at `michael@apaq.dk` for private matters.

+package dev.pathland.view.dsl
+
+import dev.pathland.view.Button as JButton
+import dev.pathland.view.View
+import dev.pathland.view.signal.Signal
+
+/** A button with a plain-text title. */
+fun Button(title: String, action: () -> Unit): View =
+    JButton.make { c -> c.title(title).action(action) }.registerChild()
+
+/** A button whose title is bound to a signal. */
+fun Button(title: Signal<String>, action: () -> Unit): View =
+    JButton.make { c -> c.title(title).action(action) }.registerChild()
+
+/**
+ * A button with a custom label: `Button(action = { save() }) { Text("Save") }`.
+ * The action is a named argument because the trailing lambda is the label.
+ */
+fun Button(action: () -> Unit, content: () -> Unit): View {
+    val children = collectChildren(content)
+    return JButton.make { c -> c.action(action) }
+        .children(*children.toTypedArray())
+        .registerChild()
+}
+
+/** A button with both a title and an explicit label subtree (the subtree wins). */
+fun Button(title: String, action: () -> Unit, content: () -> Unit): View {
+    val children = collectChildren(content)
+    return JButton.make { c -> c.title(title).action(action) }
+        .children(*children.toTypedArray())
+        .registerChild()
+}

+package dev.pathland.view.dsl
+
+import dev.pathland.view.Environment
+import dev.pathland.view.View
+import dev.pathland.view.emit.PathlandNode
+import dev.pathland.view.signal.Signal
+import dev.pathland.view.signal.Signals
+import dev.pathland.view.signal.WritableSignal
+import dev.pathland.view.state.PersistentState
+import java.util.function.UnaryOperator
+import kotlin.properties.ReadWriteProperty
+import kotlin.reflect.KProperty
+
+/**
+ * Base class for application-authored Kotlin views.
+ *
+ * A subclass declares its subtree in [body]; a signal read there re-renders only this
+ * component (the Java emitter tracks the slot). Persisted state is declared with
+ * [state] / [mutableState] and is bound to the session's [PersistentState] before the
+ * first body render — no annotation processor or kapt.
+ *
+ * Constructing a [KotlinView] inside a builder block auto-registers it, so
+ * `VStack { CounterView() }` needs no `.children(...)`.
+ */
+abstract class KotlinView : View {
+
+    private val stateSignals = mutableListOf<StateSignal<*>>()
+
+    init {
+        // Inline construction (`VStack { CounterView() }`) auto-registers. A view
+        // constructed as a field of another view must not leak into the enclosing
+        // builder scope; it is added explicitly with `+field` inside body().
+        if (!insideAnotherViewConstructor()) {
+            registerChild()
+        }
+    }
+
+    /**
+     * A persisted, two-way state signal keyed by the property name:
+     * `private var count by state(0)` or with an explicit store key
+     * `private var count by state(0, "counter")`.
+     */
+    protected fun <T : Any> state(initial: T, key: String? = null): StateDelegate<T> =
+        StateDelegate(mutableState(initial, key))
+
+    /**
+     * A persisted state signal for code that wants the signal directly:
+     * `val name = mutableState("")` can be passed to `TextField(text = name)`.
+     */
+    protected fun <T : Any> mutableState(initial: T, key: String? = null): StateSignal<T> {
+        val state = StateSignal(initial, key)
+        stateSignals.add(state)
+        return state
+    }
+
+    final override fun renderNode(env: Environment): PathlandNode {
+        env.state()?.let { persistent ->
+            stateSignals.forEach { it.bind(persistent) }
+        }
+        val resolved = body()
+        check(resolved !== this) {
+            "${javaClass.name} must return its subtree from body()"
+        }
+        return resolved.renderNode(env)
+    }
+
+    abstract override fun body(): View
+
+    private fun insideAnotherViewConstructor(): Boolean {
+        val self = javaClass
+        return java.lang.StackWalker
+            .getInstance(java.lang.StackWalker.Option.RETAIN_CLASS_REFERENCE)
+            .walk { frames ->
+                frames.anyMatch { frame ->
+                    frame.methodName == "<init>" &&
+                        frame.declaringClass != self &&
+                        frame.declaringClass != KotlinView::class.java &&
+                        KotlinView::class.java.isAssignableFrom(frame.declaringClass)
+                }
+            }
+    }
+}
+
+/**
+ * A persisted state value. It behaves as a [WritableSignal] so it can be passed
+ * straight to two-way controls; binding to the session store happens before the
+ * owning view's [KotlinView.body] runs.
+ */
+class StateSignal<T : Any> internal constructor(
+    initial: T,
+    var key: String? = null,
+) : WritableSignal<T> {
+
+    private var current: WritableSignal<T> = Signals.signal(initial)
+    private var bound = false
+
+    internal fun bind(persistent: PersistentState) {
+        if (bound) return
+        val storeKey = checkNotNull(key) { "State has no key (declare it with `by state(...)`) " }
+        current = persistent.signal(storeKey, current.get())
+        bound = true
+    }
+
+    override fun get(): T = current.get()
+
+    override fun set(value: T) = current.set(value)
+
+    override fun update(fn: UnaryOperator<T>) = current.update(fn)
+
+    override fun asReadonly(): Signal<T> = current.asReadonly()
+
+    /** The auto-saved persisted value (the signal itself is a [WritableSignal]). */
+    var value: T
+        get() = get()
+        set(value) = set(value)
+}
+
+/** Property-delegate form of [StateSignal]. */
+class StateDelegate<T : Any> internal constructor(
+    val signal: StateSignal<T>,
+) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> {
+
+    operator fun provideDelegate(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): StateDelegate<T> {
+        if (signal.key == null) {
+            signal.key = property.name
+        }
+        return this
+    }
+
+    override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T = signal.get()
+
+    override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) = signal.set(value)
+}

+package dev.pathland.view.dsl
+

+/**
+ * Build a seeded router:
+ *
+ * ```
+ * val router = navigator("/") {
+ *     route("/", HomeView())
+ *     route("/users/:id") { params -> UserView(params.intValue("id")) }
+ *     fallback(NotFoundView())
+ * }
+ * ```
+ */
+fun navigator(initialPath: String = "/", routes: Navigation.Builder.() -> Unit): Router =
+    Navigation.navigator(initialPath).apply(routes).build()
+
+/** Build a router bound to the host-provided active-path signal (deep links/popstate). */
+fun navigator(activePath: Signal<String>, routes: Navigation.Builder.() -> Unit): Router =
+    Navigation.navigator().apply(routes).build(activePath)
+
+/** The navigation slot (SwiftUI `NavigationStack` shape). */
+fun NavigationStack(
+    router: Router,
+    chrome: Chrome = Chrome.PLATFORM_DEFAULT,
+): View = Navigation.container(router, chrome).registerChild()
+
+/** Alias of [NavigationStack] using the protocol's component name. */
+fun NavigationContainer(
+    router: Router,
+    chrome: Chrome = Chrome.PLATFORM_DEFAULT,
+): View = NavigationStack(router, chrome)
+
+/** A text-labelled navigation link. */
+fun NavigationLink(
+    label: String,
+    to: String,
+    router: Router? = null,
+): View = JNavigationLink.make { c ->
+    c.label(label).to(to)
+    if (router != null) c.router(router)
+}.registerChild()
+
+/** A navigation link with a custom label subtree. */
+fun NavigationLink(
+    to: String,
+    router: Router? = null,
+    content: () -> Unit,
+): View {
+    val children = collectChildren(content)
+    val label = when (children.size) {
+        0 -> dev.pathland.view.Text.make("")
+        1 -> children[0]
+        else -> dev.pathland.view.Group.children(*children.toTypedArray())
+    }
+    return JNavigationLink.make { c ->
+        c.label(label).to(to)
+        if (router != null) c.router(router)
+    }.registerChild()
+}
+
+/** A reactive "is this the active route" signal. */
+fun isActive(router: Router, path: String): Signal<Boolean> = Navigation.isActive(router, path)
+
+/** Declare a route-change intent on any view; the emitter resolves the nearest router. */
+fun View.navigate(to: String): View = modifiers(NavigationIntent.navigate(to))
+
+/** Push onto the nearest router's back-stack. */
+fun View.push(to: String): View = modifiers(NavigationIntent.push(to))
+
+/** Replace the current route without touching the back-stack. */
+fun View.replace(to: String): View = modifiers(NavigationIntent.replace(to))

+package dev.pathland.view.dsl
+
+import dev.pathland.view.View
+import java.util.ArrayDeque
+
+/**
+ * Marks the Kotlin DSL entry points. The builder is synchronous and single-threaded
+ * (the same contract as the emitter and the Java environment), so a thread-local
+ * child stack is the equivalent of SwiftUI's result builder.
+ */
+@DslMarker
+annotation class PathlandDsl
+
+internal object ViewScopes {
+    private val stack = ThreadLocal.withInitial { ArrayDeque<MutableList<View>>() }
+
+    fun push(): MutableList<View> {
+        val scope = mutableListOf<View>()
+        stack.get().addLast(scope)
+        return scope
+    }
+
+    fun pop() {
+        stack.get().removeLast()
+    }
+
+    fun current(): MutableList<View>? = stack.get().peekLast()
+
+    fun register(view: View) {
+        val scope = current() ?: return
+        if (scope.none { it === view }) {
+            scope.add(view)
+        }
+    }
+}
+
+/**
+ * Add a view built outside the DSL builders (e.g. a Java `View` or
+ * `mediaController.attach()`) to the current block.
+ */
+fun View.add(): View = registerChild()
+
+/** Prefix form: `+mediaController.attach()`. */
+operator fun View.unaryPlus(): View = registerChild()
+
+/**
+ * Collect the views declared by [content]. A newly declared child auto-registers
+ * into the innermost active scope, so `VStack { Text("a"); Text("b") }` needs no
+ * `.children(...)` boilerplate.
+ */
+fun collectChildren(content: () -> Unit): List<View> {
+    val scope = ViewScopes.push()
+    return try {
+        content()
+        scope.toList()
+    } finally {
+        ViewScopes.pop()
+    }
+}
+
+internal fun <T : View> T.registerChild(): T {
+    ViewScopes.register(this)
+    return this
+}
+
+/** Collect a ForEach row into one child view (a single child stays unwrapped). */
+internal fun rowView(content: () -> Unit): View {
+    val children = collectChildren(content)
+    return when (children.size) {
+        0 -> dev.pathland.view.Group.children()
+        1 -> children[0]
+        else -> dev.pathland.view.Group.children(*children.toTypedArray())
+    }
+}

+val <T> Signal<T>.value: T
+    get() = get()
+
+/** A two-way signal value: `count.value = 1`, `count.value += 1`. */
+var <T> WritableSignal<T>.value: T
+    get() = get()
+    set(value) = set(value)
+
+/** Derive a read-only signal from this one. */
+fun <T, R> Signal<T>.map(transform: (T) -> R): Signal<R> =

+fun <T> WritableSignal<T>.readonly(): Signal<T> = asReadonly()

+package dev.pathland.view.dsl
+
+import dev.pathland.view.Categories
